strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and previously open theoretical question: why Byzantine failures empirically generalize worse than data poisoning despite prior results showing comparable optimization guarantees. The paper convincingly explains this gap via a stability-based analysis.

Rigorous theory with matching (up to log/constant factors) upper and lower bounds on uniform stability for data poisoning (Theorems 3.3, 3.4), and a non-trivial lower bound for Byzantine failures (Theorem 3.2) in the regime f in [n/3, n/2), establishing a genuine order-of-magnitude separation between the two threat models.

Technically interesting proof machinery, notably Lemma D.1 characterizing the SMEA aggregation rule's behavior on collinear gradient vectors, which is reused across several lower-bound constructions and could be of independent interest for future robust-aggregation analyses.

The paper connects stability bounds to actual generalization error (not just an upper bound but a matching construction, Lemma 4.1/Theorem 4.2), and its numerical experiment (Figure 1) corroborates the theoretical predictions, including matching constants under data poisoning.

Clear, honest discussion of limitations and open questions (Section H and future work list): the paper explicitly notes that the tight Byzantine lower bound only holds for f ≥ n/3, that other aggregation rules/algorithms (momentum, multi-step methods) are not formally analyzed, and discusses why optimization vs. generalization differ conceptually.
Reasonably thorough related-work positioning, clarifying differences from Farhadkhani et al. (2024b), Farhadkhani et al. (2022b), and Ye & Ling (2025).
weaknesses: The headline claim of a 'fundamental gap' is rigorously established only for f in [n/3, n/2); for the practically important regime f < n/3, the paper has no matching Byzantine lower bound and relies solely on limited numerical evidence (Section 4) to argue the gap persists, which weakens the generality of the central claim.

Nearly all tightness results (both upper and lower bounds) are specific to the SMEA aggregation rule; while the paper argues some proof ideas generalize, the concrete matching-bound results do not obviously extend to other widely used robust aggregators (e.g., trimmed mean, Krum, CClip), limiting the scope of the 'fundamental' separation claim.

Empirical validation is very limited: a single small-scale (n=15) synthetic instantiation that essentially replicates the exact worst-case construction used in the theoretical proofs, rather than independent experiments on realistic datasets/models with standard/adaptive attacks; this makes it hard to assess how much the gap manifests in practical (non-worst-case) distributed learning settings.

The stability constructions rely on quite pathological loss functions and point-mass/two-point data distributions (e.g., linear losses, Dirac mixtures) that are common in the stability-analysis literature but are far from realistic loss landscapes, making it less clear how tightly these theoretical rates predict practical generalization gaps for, e.g., deep networks.

The paper does not formally extend results to momentum-based, variance-reduced, or multi-local-step algorithms (FedAvg-style), which are the most practically relevant distributed learning methods; these are deferred to future work with only informal arguments in the appendix.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy even by theory-paper standards, which may limit accessibility; some intuitive explanations (e.g., 'why optimization is unaffected but generalization is') would benefit from earlier, more prominent placement in the main text rather than being pushed to Section 4/discussion.
